result: The study used single-genome proviral sequencing to analyze HIV-1 proviral sequences from autopsy samples of three ART-treated participants, collecting tissue from up to 18 different organ systems including CNS tissues. A total of 1471.73 million cells were analyzed, yielding 1497 amplified proviral sequences, of which 497 were selected for next-generation sequencing based on amplicon size.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the methodological approach, with one stating 'the sophisticated near-full length sequencing technique that allows for inferences about genetic intactness and clonality of proviruses' is a strength, and another noting 'this is a study that is technically demanding and here is well done.' The editor describes the study as using 'near full-length HIV-1 sequencing' and finds the results 'convincing.'

result: 48 genome-intact proviruses (3.21% of all proviruses) were identified, with the highest frequencies in lymph nodes (0.52-0.58 intact proviruses/million cells in participants 1 and 2), followed by gastrointestinal and genitourinary tissues. Many sequences showed evidence of clonal proliferation, consistent with prior studies.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without challenge. The editor states 'Intact as well as defective HIV-1 proviruses are found at various anatomical sites including the central nervous system; the results are convincing.' One reviewer notes 'there is a lot of data here to draw many useful conclusions,' implicitly accepting the intact provirus findings.

result: Intact proviruses were detected in CNS tissues of participants 1 and 3, specifically in the basal ganglia (0.015-0.030 intact proviruses/million cells) and periventricular white matter (0.027 intact proviruses/million cells in participant 3). This represents the first documentation of genome-intact proviral sequences in CNS tissues using near full-length proviral sequencing, though frequencies were comparatively low compared to lymphoid tissues.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. The editor states the results are 'relevant for our understanding of latent viral reservoirs, especially in the brain.' One reviewer notes 'They identified clonally expanded proviruses in the CNS in all three individuals' as a key finding. Another reviewer acknowledges the study provides 'insights that prompt new and more sophisticated questions' about CNS reservoirs.

result: Defective proviral sequences were detected in nearly all analyzed tissue samples, with highest frequencies in lymph nodes (5.7-13.0 defective proviruses/million cells). The prostate showed very high frequencies of virally infected cells in participant 2, second only to lymph nodes. CNS tissues contained relatively low frequencies compared to other sites.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings. The editor's statement that 'Intact as well as defective HIV-1 proviruses are found at various anatomical sites' implicitly accepts the defective provirus distribution data. No reviewer raises concerns about the tissue distribution patterns reported.

result: Large clones of intact proviruses were observed across multiple tissues in participants 1 and 2. Notably, in participant 1, one clone included intact proviral sequences from basal ganglia and lymph node tissues, representing the first demonstration of CNS tissue involvement in multi-compartment dissemination of large clones of HIV-1 proviruses in ART-treated persons.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the clonality findings. One reviewer states 'It will be important to realize how clones of infected T cells can move around the body, including into the CNS compartment,' acknowledging the multi-compartment clonal dissemination. Another notes the study allows 'inferences about genetic intactness and clonality of proviruses' as a strength.

result: Clonal proviral sequences in CNS tissues were detected in all three participants, with clones distributed across different CNS regions (basal ganglia, frontal lobe, thalamus, occipital lobe, periventricular white matter). In participant 3, one large clone involving 9 defective sequences was broadly distributed across multiple brain regions, suggesting local spread through clonal proliferation within the CNS immune microenvironment.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings. One reviewer explicitly states 'They identified clonally expanded proviruses in the CNS in all three individuals' as a key result. The editor describes the results as 'convincing and relevant for our understanding of latent viral reservoirs, especially in the brain,' implicitly accepting the CNS clonality data.

result: All proviral sequences from participants 1 and 3 were predicted to be CCR5-tropic, while 62.1% of sequences from participant 2 were CXCR4-tropic. Participant 2 had delayed ART initiation (25 years after diagnosis) and died 10 months after starting treatment, likely explaining the coreceptor switch. CXCR4-tropic proviruses in participant 2 were predominantly found in prostate, spleen, and lymph nodes, with minimal CNS presence.
evaluation: One reviewer raises a significant concern: 'it is important to emphasize that there is another entry phenotype beyond X4 that will ultimately be important in interpreting these results. Macrophage-tropic viruses are often found in the CNS compartment and it will be important to understand whether these CNS-derived sequences are macrophage-tropic viruses.' This indicates the tropism analysis may be incomplete and interpretation uncertain.

result: The frequency of viral amino acid residues associated with resistance to broadly neutralizing antibodies did not differ notably among tissue compartments, and no sequence variations consistent with antiretroviral drug resistance were observed in intact proviral sequences.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings. The lack of drug resistance mutations is consistent with the clinical data showing adherence to ART, which reviewers accept without question.

result: The study could not determine which cell types harbor HIV-1 in the CNS and are responsible for clonal expansion. The authors speculate that infected microglia may be involved due to their long half-life, self-renewal capacity, and high HIV-1 susceptibility, though migrating CD4 T cells acting as 'Trojan horses' is also possible.
evaluation: One reviewer explicitly states 'it is unclear which cell types these viruses persist in' and notes 'Cell type identification would greatly enhance the impact of this work.' Another reviewer emphasizes the need to understand 'whether these CNS-derived sequences are macrophage-tropic viruses there infecting macrophages and microglia or if they are all T-tropic viruses brought in by wandering infected T cells (or both).' This indicates significant uncertainty about cellular origins.

result: The study has several acknowledged limitations: only 3 participants, limited tissue availability from participant 3, very few cells assayed from terminal ileum and testes, no peripheral blood samples available, and potential contamination of tissue samples with peripheral blood cells (though washing procedures were employed and lack of intact proviruses in liver argues against contamination).
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge and emphasize these limitations. One states 'The small sample size (n=3) is a drawback' and notes 'two individuals were on ART for just one year at the time of autopsy and had T cells compatible with AIDS, and one of these individuals had a low-level detectable viral load,' questioning generalizability. Another reviewer notes 'it is possible that these reservoir cells might have been infiltrating T cells from blood present at the time of autopsy tissue sampling.'

result: The study provides a deep analysis of tissue reservoirs for HIV-1 including detailed assessment of CNS tissues, supporting the persistence of genome-intact HIV-1 in many tissues including the CNS. The findings emphasize difficulties in eliminating HIV-1 from the human body and will inform HIV-1 cure strategies.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the study's contributions. The editor calls it 'important' with results that are 'convincing and relevant for our understanding of latent viral reservoirs.' One reviewer states the study 'contributes to our understanding of the tissue distribution of persistent HIV-1, and informs the ongoing search for viral eradication.' Another notes it 'is well done, providing insights that prompt new and more sophisticated questions.'
